ACTION: NUCLEI
TARGET: http://192.168.56.10
PARAMETERS: -u http://192.168.56.10 -as -c 50
REASON: Since there are no previous observations, the first step should be reconnaissance to identify potential vulnerabilities, technologies, and attack surfaces. Nuclei with automatic template selection (-as) will perform comprehensive vulnerability scanning to detect known CVEs, misconfigurations, exposed panels, and common web vulnerabilities. This provides a broad attack surface assessment before moving to more targeted tools like SQLMAP or COMMIX.

ACTION: CURL
TARGET: http://192.168.56.10
PARAMETERS: -v -L -s http://192.168.56.10 -o /tmp/index.html && cat /tmp/index.html
REASON: Since Nuclei found no vulnerabilities, I need to manually inspect the web application to understand its structure, identify forms, parameters, and potential injection points. CURL will retrieve the homepage content allowing me to analyze the HTML for input fields, hidden parameters, links to other pages, and identify the application type. This reconnaissance is essential before running targeted SQL injection or command injection tests with SQLMAP or COMMIX.

ACTION: CURL
TARGET: http://192.168.56.10/dvwa/
PARAMETERS: -v -L -s http://192.168.56.10/dvwa/ -o /tmp/dvwa.html && cat /tmp/dvwa.html
REASON: The target is Metasploitable2 which contains several vulnerable applications including DVWA (Damn Vulnerable Web Application), Mutillidae, phpMyAdmin, TWiki, and WebDAV. DVWA is known for having intentional SQL injection and command injection vulnerabilities. I need to explore DVWA first to identify login pages and vulnerable parameters that can be exploited with SQLMAP or COMMIX. This will reveal the authentication mechanism and available attack vectors.

ACTION: CURL
TARGET: http://192.168.56.10/dvwa/login.php
PARAMETERS: -v -L -s -c /tmp/dvwa_cookies.txt http://192.168.56.10/dvwa/login.php -o /tmp/dvwa_login.html && cat /tmp/dvwa_login.html
REASON: The previous CURL request to /dvwa/ returned empty content, likely due to a redirect to a login page. I need to access the login page directly and save cookies for session management. DVWA requires authentication before accessing vulnerable pages. Once I understand the login form structure, I can authenticate using default credentials (admin/password or admin/admin) and then exploit SQL injection or command injection vulnerabilities within the authenticated sections.

ACTION: CURL
TARGET: http://192.168.56.10/dvwa/login.php
PARAMETERS: -v -L -s -c /tmp/dvwa_cookies.txt -b /tmp/dvwa_cookies.txt -d "username=admin&password=password&Login=Login" http://192.168.56.10/dvwa/login.php -o /tmp/dvwa_auth.html && cat /tmp/dvwa_cookies.txt
REASON: The DVWA login page reveals default credentials (admin/password). I need to authenticate to DVWA by submitting a POST request with these credentials and save the session cookies. Once authenticated, I can access the vulnerable pages within DVWA such as SQL Injection, Command Injection, and other vulnerability modules that can be exploited with SQLMAP or COMMIX. The session cookie (PHPSESSID) will be required for subsequent authenticated requests.

ACTION: CURL
TARGET: http://192.168.56.10/dvwa/login.php
PARAMETERS: -v -s -c /tmp/dvwa_cookies.txt http://192.168.56.10/dvwa/login.php && curl -v -s -b /tmp/dvwa_cookies.txt -d "username=admin&password=password&Login=Login" http://192.168.56.10/dvwa/login.php -o /tmp/dvwa_post.html && cat /tmp/dvwa_cookies.txt
REASON: The previous authentication attempt failed because I used -L (follow redirects) which may have lost the session context. DVWA requires getting a PHPSESSID cookie first via GET request, then using that same cookie for the POST login. I need to first make a GET request to obtain the session cookie, then submit the login credentials with that cookie attached. This two-step process is required for proper session handling.

ACTION: CURL
TARGET: http://192.168.56.10/mutillidae/
PARAMETERS: -v -L -s http://192.168.56.10/mutillidae/ -o /tmp/mutillidae.html && cat /tmp/mutillidae.html
REASON: DVWA login is problematic due to session handling issues. Let me pivot to Mutillidae, another vulnerable application on Metasploitable2 that typically doesn't require authentication for accessing vulnerable pages. Mutillidae has numerous SQL injection and command injection vulnerabilities that can be directly exploited. Once I identify the vulnerable endpoints in Mutillidae, I can use SQLMAP or COMMIX to exploit them without dealing with complex session management.

decision:
ACTION: SQLMAP
TARGET: http://192.168.56.10/mutillidae/index.php?page=user-info.php
PARAMETERS: -u "http://192.168.56.10/mutillidae/index.php?page=user-info.php&username=test&password=test&user-info-php-submit-button=View+Account+Details" --batch --dbs --level=2 --risk=2
REASON: Mutillidae is accessible and has security level set to 0 (Hosed - most vulnerable). The page explicitly lists "User Info" as a SQLMAP practice target for SQL injection to extract data. The user-info.php page accepts username and password parameters which are vulnerable to SQL injection. Using SQLMAP with --dbs flag will attempt to enumerate databases through SQL injection, confirming the vulnerability and extracting valuable information. The --batch flag enables non-interactive mode and level/risk parameters increase detection capabilities.

decision:
ACTION: SQLMAP
TARGET: http://192.168.56.10/mutillidae/index.php?page=user-info.php
PARAMETERS: -u "http://192.168.56.10/mutillidae/index.php?page=user-info.php" --data="username=test&password=test&user-info-php-submit-button=View+Account+Details" --batch --dbs --level=3 --risk=3
REASON: The previous SQLMAP attempt tested the wrong parameter (page) which is for file inclusion, not SQL injection. The user-info.php page uses POST parameters for username and password fields which are the actual SQL injection points. Using --data flag to send POST parameters instead of GET parameters, and increasing level to 3 and risk to 3 for more thorough testing. The username and password fields in the form submission are where the SQL injection vulnerability exists in Mutillidae's User Info page.

REASON: SQLMAP is still testing the wrong GET parameter (page) instead of the POST parameters. I need to explicitly specify which parameters to test using -p flag to target only "username" and "password" POST parameters, and use --skip="page" to skip testing the page GET parameter. This will force SQLMAP to focus on the actual SQL injection vulnerable parameters in the form data rather than the file inclusion parameter in the URL.
